## Introduction

::: {.callout}

MaxDiff, also called Best-Worst Scaling, is a survey method for measuring relative preferences. Instead of asking respondents to rate each item on a numeric scale, the survey repeatedly shows a small set of items and asks for two choices: the most-preferred item and the least-preferred item. In this survey, each valid MaxDiff screen shows 4 MSBA classes.

MaxDiff is useful because people are generally better at making trade-offs than at calibrating rating scales. For example, two students may both give several classes a 7 out of 10, but those 7s may not mean the same thing. A best-worst task forces differentiation: when four classes appear together, the respondent must decide which one is strongest and which one is weakest. This reduces scale-use bias and gives us information about preference ordering.

In this assignment, the items are 10 core MSBA classes at UCSD Rady. I estimate relative preference using three approaches. First, I compute a simple counts score: the percentage of times each class is chosen best minus the percentage of times it is chosen worst. Second, I estimate a multinomial logit (MNL) model by maximum likelihood. Third, I estimate the same MNL model using a Bayesian random-walk Metropolis-Hastings sampler.

I expect the three methods to agree on the broad story, especially at the top and bottom of the ranking. They should differ most in the middle, where classes have similar preference strength and small changes in estimation method can flip the order. The MNL and Bayesian methods also give a more formal way to quantify uncertainty than the simple counts score.

:::


## The Data

::: {.callout-}

The data file is organized at the item-task level: each row is one class shown to one respondent on one MaxDiff screen. I first read the response file and the item-label file, then standardize the column names. One important cleaning step is needed: the raw file contains both 4-item MaxDiff tasks and later 2-item choice tasks. Since this assignment is about MaxDiff, I keep only tasks that have exactly four rows, one best choice, one worst choice, and two unchosen items.

```{python}
#| label: data-read-clean-check
#| echo: false

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 80)

# Read raw files
choices_raw = pd.read_csv("maxdiff_design_and_choices.csv")
item_labels_raw = pd.read_csv("maxdiff_item_labels.csv")

# Clean column names in the choice data
choices = choices_raw.rename(columns={
    "Record ID": "record_id",
    "Task": "task",
    "Position": "position",
    "Item": "item",
    "Response": "response"
}).copy()

choices["record_id"] = choices["record_id"].astype(str)

for col in ["task", "position", "item", "response"]:
    choices[col] = pd.to_numeric(choices[col], errors="raise").astype(int)

# Clean item labels
item_labels = (
    item_labels_raw
    .rename(columns={
        "Item #": "item",
        "Item": "item_label"
    })
    .loc[:, ["item", "item_label"]]
    .copy()
)

item_labels["item"] = pd.to_numeric(item_labels["item"], errors="raise").astype(int)

display(Markdown("### Item labels"))
display(item_labels)
```

The table below checks the raw task structure before filtering. A valid MaxDiff task should have 4 rows, exactly one `Response = 1`, exactly one `Response = -1`, and two rows with `Response = 0`.

```{python}
#| label: raw-task-structure
#| echo: false

valid_items = set(item_labels["item"])

task_check_raw = (
    choices
    .groupby(["record_id", "task"])
    .agg(
        n_rows=("response", "size"),
        n_best=("response", lambda x: (x == 1).sum()),
        n_worst=("response", lambda x: (x == -1).sum()),
        n_zero=("response", lambda x: (x == 0).sum()),
        all_items_labeled=("item", lambda x: x.isin(valid_items).all())
    )
    .reset_index()
)

task_check_raw["valid_maxdiff_task"] = (
    (task_check_raw["n_rows"] == 4)
    & (task_check_raw["n_best"] == 1)
    & (task_check_raw["n_worst"] == 1)
    & (task_check_raw["n_zero"] == 2)
    & (task_check_raw["all_items_labeled"])
)

raw_task_patterns = (
    task_check_raw
    .groupby([
        "n_rows",
        "n_best",
        "n_worst",
        "n_zero",
        "all_items_labeled",
        "valid_maxdiff_task"
    ])
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="n_tasks")
    .sort_values(["valid_maxdiff_task", "n_rows"], ascending=[False, True])
)

display(Markdown("### Raw task pattern check"))
display(raw_task_patterns)

# Keep only valid 4-item MaxDiff tasks
valid_task_keys = task_check_raw.loc[
    task_check_raw["valid_maxdiff_task"],
    ["record_id", "task"]
]

maxdiff = (
    choices
    .merge(valid_task_keys, on=["record_id", "task"], how="inner")
    .merge(item_labels, on="item", how="left")
    .sort_values(["record_id", "task", "position"])
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

n_raw_tasks = len(task_check_raw)
n_valid_tasks = len(valid_task_keys)
n_dropped_tasks = n_raw_tasks - n_valid_tasks

display(Markdown(
    f"The raw data contain **{len(choices_raw):,} rows** across **{n_raw_tasks:,} respondent-task combinations**. "
    f"After keeping only valid 4-item MaxDiff tasks, the analysis data contain **{len(maxdiff):,} rows** "
    f"from **{n_valid_tasks:,} MaxDiff tasks**. "
    f"The remaining **{n_dropped_tasks:,} tasks** are dropped because they are not 4-item MaxDiff tasks."
))
```

```{python}
#| label: basic-descriptives

respondent_task_counts = (

items_per_task = (

    if len(values) == 1:
        return values[0]

N = maxdiff["record_id"].nunique()
T = one_value_or_range(respondent_task_counts)

basic_descriptives = pd.DataFrame({
    "metric": [
        "Respondents (N)",

        "Total study items",

        "Valid MaxDiff rows"
    ],
    "value": [
        N,
        T,
        J,
        n_study_items,
        n_valid_tasks,

})

display(basic_descriptives)
```

The cleaned data pass the MaxDiff sanity check: every task has exactly one best choice, exactly one worst choice, and two unchosen alternatives.

```{python}
#| label: sanity-check-cleaned-data
#| echo: false

sanity_check = (
    maxdiff
    .groupby(["record_id", "task"])
    .agg(
        n_rows=("response", "size"),
        n_best=("response", lambda x: (x == 1).sum()),
        n_worst=("response", lambda x: (x == -1).sum()),
        n_zero=("response", lambda x: (x == 0).sum())
    )
    .reset_index()
)

sanity_check["passes_check"] = (
    (sanity_check["n_rows"] == 4)
    & (sanity_check["n_best"] == 1)
    & (sanity_check["n_worst"] == 1)
    & (sanity_check["n_zero"] == 2)
)

sanity_summary = (
    sanity_check["passes_check"]
    .value_counts()
    .rename_axis("passes_check")
    .reset_index(name="n_tasks")
)

display(sanity_summary)

# Stop the render if the cleaned MaxDiff data are not valid
assert sanity_check["passes_check"].all()
```

Finally, I report how often each item was shown. The exposure counts are similar across the 10 classes, which is what we expect from a balanced MaxDiff design.

```{python}
#| label: item-exposure
#| echo: false

shown_counts = (
    maxdiff
    .groupby(["item", "item_label"])
    .agg(
        times_shown=("item", "size"),
        times_best=("response", lambda x: (x == 1).sum()),
        times_worst=("response", lambda x: (x == -1).sum())
    )
    .reset_index()
    .sort_values("item")
)

display(shown_counts)

min_shown = shown_counts["times_shown"].min()
max_shown = shown_counts["times_shown"].max()

display(Markdown(

))
```

## Counts Analysis

::: {.callout-}
The first method is a simple counts analysis. For each class, I calculate how often it was selected as the most-preferred class when it appeared, and how often it was selected as the least-preferred class when it appeared. The counts score is the difference between these two percentages:

$$
\text{score}_j = \%\text{best}_j - \%\text{worst}_j
$$

A score close to +1 means that a class is almost always chosen as the best option when shown. A score close to -1 means that it is almost always chosen as the worst option when shown. A score near 0 means that the class is either middle-of-the-pack or receives mixed reactions from respondents.

```{python}
#| label: counts-analysis-table
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

from IPython.display import display, Markdown, HTML
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Count how often each item was shown, picked best, and picked worst
counts_table = (
    maxdiff
    .groupby(["item", "item_label"])
    .agg(
        times_shown=("response", "size"),
        times_best=("response", lambda x: int((x == 1).sum())),
        times_worst=("response", lambda x: int((x == -1).sum()))
    )
    .reset_index()
)

counts_table["pct_best"] = counts_table["times_best"] / counts_table["times_shown"]
counts_table["pct_worst"] = counts_table["times_worst"] / counts_table["times_shown"]
counts_table["score"] = counts_table["pct_best"] - counts_table["pct_worst"]

# Sort from most preferred to least preferred
counts_table = (
    counts_table
    .sort_values("score", ascending=False)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

counts_table["counts_rank"] = np.arange(1, len(counts_table) + 1)

# Bootstrap confidence intervals by resampling respondents
rng = np.random.default_rng(403)
n_boot = 1000

items = np.array(sorted(maxdiff["item"].unique()))
respondents = np.array(sorted(maxdiff["record_id"].unique()))
n_resp = len(respondents)
n_items = len(items)

shown_mat = np.zeros((n_resp, n_items))
best_mat = np.zeros((n_resp, n_items))
worst_mat = np.zeros((n_resp, n_items))

for i, respondent in enumerate(respondents):
    sub = maxdiff[maxdiff["record_id"] == respondent]

    shown_counts_i = sub.groupby("item").size().reindex(items, fill_value=0)
    best_counts_i = sub[sub["response"] == 1].groupby("item").size().reindex(items, fill_value=0)
    worst_counts_i = sub[sub["response"] == -1].groupby("item").size().reindex(items, fill_value=0)

    shown_mat[i, :] = shown_counts_i.values
    best_mat[i, :] = best_counts_i.values
    worst_mat[i, :] = worst_counts_i.values

boot_scores = np.zeros((n_boot, n_items))

for b in range(n_boot):
    sampled_rows = rng.integers(0, n_resp, size=n_resp)

    shown_b = shown_mat[sampled_rows, :].sum(axis=0)
    best_b = best_mat[sampled_rows, :].sum(axis=0)
    worst_b = worst_mat[sampled_rows, :].sum(axis=0)

    boot_scores[b, :] = (best_b / shown_b) - (worst_b / shown_b)

ci_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "item": items,
    "ci_lower": np.percentile(boot_scores, 2.5, axis=0),
    "ci_upper": np.percentile(boot_scores, 97.5, axis=0)
})

counts_table = counts_table.merge(ci_table, on="item", how="left")

# Display table
counts_display = counts_table.copy()
counts_display["pct_best"] = (100 * counts_display["pct_best"]).round(1).astype(str) + "%"
counts_display["pct_worst"] = (100 * counts_display["pct_worst"]).round(1).astype(str) + "%"
counts_display["score"] = counts_display["score"].round(3)
counts_display["ci_lower"] = counts_display["ci_lower"].round(3)
counts_display["ci_upper"] = counts_display["ci_upper"].round(3)

counts_display = counts_display[[
    "counts_rank",
    "item",
    "item_label",
    "times_shown",
    "times_best",
    "times_worst",
    "pct_best",
    "pct_worst",
    "score",
    "ci_lower",
    "ci_upper"
]]

counts_display = counts_display.rename(columns={
    "counts_rank": "Rank",
    "item": "Item",
    "item_label": "Class",
    "times_shown": "Times shown",
    "times_best": "Times best",
    "times_worst": "Times worst",
    "pct_best": "% best",
    "pct_worst": "% worst",
    "score": "Counts score",
    "ci_lower": "95% CI lower",
    "ci_upper": "95% CI upper"
})

display(HTML(counts_display.to_html(index=False)))
```

The ranked table shows a clear spread in student preferences. Classes with positive scores were selected as best more often than worst, while classes with negative scores were selected as worst more often than best.

```{python}
#| echo: false
```

```{python}
top3 = counts_table.head(3)
bottom3 = counts_table.tail(3).sort_values("score", ascending=True)
```

## From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices

::: {.callout-}
The MaxDiff responses can be treated as multinomial logit choice data. In each task, a respondent sees four classes and makes two choices. First, they choose the class they like the most from the full set of four. Then, after the best class is removed, they choose the class they like the least from the remaining three.

For the best-choice part, the MNL model assigns each item $j$ a utility coefficient $\beta_j$. If the task shows items $\{a,b,c,d\}$, the probability that item $b$ is chosen as best is:

$$
P(\text{best}=b)
=
\frac{\exp(\beta_b)}
{\exp(\beta_a)+\exp(\beta_b)+\exp(\beta_c)+\exp(\beta_d)}
$$

For the worst-choice part, I use the same utilities but flip the sign. Intuitively, an item with high positive utility should be unlikely to be selected as worst, while an item with low utility should be more likely to be selected as worst. If item $b$ was already selected as best, then the probability that item $c$ is selected as worst from the remaining items is:

$$
P(\text{worst}=c \mid \text{best}=b)
=
\frac{\exp(-\beta_c)}
{\exp(-\beta_a)+\exp(-\beta_c)+\exp(-\beta_d)}
$$

Therefore, each MaxDiff task contributes two MNL choice observations: one best-choice observation from four alternatives, and one worst-choice observation from the remaining three alternatives.

The model also needs a normalization for identification. Adding the same constant to every $\beta_j$ would not change any of the MNL probabilities, so the absolute level of utility is not identified. I set $\beta_1 = 0$ and estimate the remaining nine coefficients, $\beta_2,\ldots,\beta_{10}$, relative to item 1.

```{python}
#| label: reshape-maxdiff-to-mnl
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

from IPython.display import display, Markdown, HTML

# Build one row per respondent-task.
# Each row stores the 4 shown items, the best item, the worst item,
# and the remaining 3 items after the best item is removed.

task_rows = []

for (record_id, task), g in maxdiff.groupby(["record_id", "task"], sort=False):
    g = g.sort_values("position")

    shown_items = tuple(g["item"].astype(int).tolist())
    best_item = int(g.loc[g["response"] == 1, "item"].iloc[0])
    worst_item = int(g.loc[g["response"] == -1, "item"].iloc[0])
    remaining_after_best = tuple([item for item in shown_items if item != best_item])

    task_rows.append({
        "record_id": record_id,
        "task": int(task),
        "shown_items": shown_items,
        "best_item": best_item,
        "worst_item": worst_item,
        "remaining_after_best": remaining_after_best
    })

choice_tasks = pd.DataFrame(task_rows)

# Create a long-format MNL dataset.
# For best observations, utility enters as +beta.
# For worst observations, utility enters as -beta.

mnl_rows = []

for row in choice_tasks.itertuples(index=False):
    best_obs_id = f"{row.record_id}_{row.task}_best"

    for item in row.shown_items:
        mnl_rows.append({
            "obs_id": best_obs_id,
            "record_id": row.record_id,
            "task": row.task,
            "choice_type": "best",
            "item": int(item),
            "chosen": int(item == row.best_item),
            "utility_sign": 1
        })

    worst_obs_id = f"{row.record_id}_{row.task}_worst"

    for item in row.remaining_after_best:
        mnl_rows.append({
            "obs_id": worst_obs_id,
            "record_id": row.record_id,
            "task": row.task,
            "choice_type": "worst",
            "item": int(item),
            "chosen": int(item == row.worst_item),
            "utility_sign": -1
        })

mnl_long = pd.DataFrame(mnl_rows).merge(item_labels, on="item", how="left")

# Arrays used later in the likelihood function.
# These use zero-based item indices: item 1 becomes index 0, item 10 becomes index 9.

all_items = np.array(sorted(item_labels["item"].unique()), dtype=int)
item_to_index = {item: idx for idx, item in enumerate(all_items)}

shown_items = np.array(choice_tasks["shown_items"].tolist(), dtype=int)
remaining_items = np.array(choice_tasks["remaining_after_best"].tolist(), dtype=int)
best_items = choice_tasks["best_item"].to_numpy(dtype=int)
worst_items = choice_tasks["worst_item"].to_numpy(dtype=int)

shown_idx = np.array([[item_to_index[item] for item in row] for row in shown_items], dtype=int)
remaining_idx = np.array([[item_to_index[item] for item in row] for row in remaining_items], dtype=int)
best_idx = np.array([item_to_index[item] for item in best_items], dtype=int)
worst_idx = np.array([item_to_index[item] for item in worst_items], dtype=int)

# Check that each MNL choice observation has exactly one chosen alternative.

mnl_obs_check = (
    mnl_long
    .groupby(["choice_type", "obs_id"])
    .agg(
        n_alternatives=("item", "size"),
        n_chosen=("chosen", "sum")
    )
    .reset_index()
)

assert (mnl_obs_check["n_chosen"] == 1).all()
assert set(mnl_obs_check.loc[mnl_obs_check["choice_type"] == "best", "n_alternatives"]) == {4}
assert set(mnl_obs_check.loc[mnl_obs_check["choice_type"] == "worst", "n_alternatives"]) == {3}

mnl_summary = (
    mnl_obs_check
    .groupby("choice_type")
    .agg(
        choice_observations=("obs_id", "nunique"),
        min_alternatives=("n_alternatives", "min"),
        max_alternatives=("n_alternatives", "max"),
        chosen_per_observation=("n_chosen", "mean")
    )
    .reset_index()
)

mnl_summary["choice_type"] = mnl_summary["choice_type"].map({
    "best": "Best choice",
    "worst": "Worst choice"
})

mnl_summary = mnl_summary.rename(columns={
    "choice_type": "Choice observation",
    "choice_observations": "Number of observations",
    "min_alternatives": "Minimum alternatives",
    "max_alternatives": "Maximum alternatives",
    "chosen_per_observation": "Chosen alternatives per observation"
})

display(HTML(mnl_summary.to_html(index=False)))

total_mnl_obs = mnl_obs_check["obs_id"].nunique()

display(Markdown(
    f"After reshaping, the **{len(choice_tasks):,} valid MaxDiff tasks** become "
    f"**{total_mnl_obs:,} MNL choice observations**: "
    f"one best-choice observation and one worst-choice observation for each task. "
    "This task-level structure will be used in the likelihood function in the next section."
))
```
:::


## MNL via Maximum Likelihood

::: {.callout-}
Next, I estimate the MNL model by maximum likelihood. Each item has a utility coefficient $\beta_j$, with item 1 used as the reference category. Therefore, I set $\beta_1 = 0$ and estimate the remaining nine coefficients.

For each MaxDiff task, the log-likelihood combines the probability of the best choice and the probability of the worst choice. The log-likelihood is:

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta})
=
\sum_{\text{tasks}}
\left[
\beta_{j_b^*}
-
\log \sum_{j \in \text{shown}} \exp(\beta_j)
-
\beta_{j_w^*}
-
\log \sum_{j \in \text{shown} \setminus \{j_b^*\}} \exp(-\beta_j)
\right]
$$

where $j_b^*$ is the item chosen as best and $j_w^*$ is the item chosen as worst. I maximize this log-likelihood using BFGS. For interpretation, I also convert the utility estimates into shares of preference:

$$
\hat{s}_j
=
\frac{\exp(\hat{\beta}_j)}
{\sum_{k=1}^{10} \exp(\hat{\beta}_k)}
$$

These shares can be interpreted as the model-implied probability that each class would be chosen if all 10 classes appeared together on one screen.

```{python}
#| label: mle-mnl-estimation
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

from scipy.special import logsumexp
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from IPython.display import display, Markdown, HTML

# Helper function:
# The optimizer estimates beta_2 through beta_10.
# beta_1 is fixed to 0 for identification.

def unpack_beta(theta):
    return np.concatenate(([0.0], np.asarray(theta, dtype=float)))


def mnl_log_likelihood(theta):
    beta = unpack_beta(theta)

    # Best-choice contribution
    best_utility = beta[best_idx]
    best_log_denom = logsumexp(beta[shown_idx], axis=1)

    # Worst-choice contribution.
    # Utilities are flipped, so worst choice uses -beta.
    worst_utility = -beta[worst_idx]
    worst_log_denom = logsumexp(-beta[remaining_idx], axis=1)

    ll_value = np.sum(
        best_utility
        - best_log_denom
        + worst_utility
        - worst_log_denom
    )

    return float(ll_value)


def mnl_gradient(theta):
    beta = unpack_beta(theta)
    grad_full = np.zeros_like(beta)

    # Gradient for best-choice part:
    # chosen indicator minus softmax probabilities over shown items.
    best_u = beta[shown_idx]
    best_prob = np.exp(best_u - logsumexp(best_u, axis=1, keepdims=True))

    np.add.at(grad_full, best_idx, 1.0)

    for position in range(shown_idx.shape[1]):
        np.add.at(
            grad_full,
            shown_idx[:, position],
            -best_prob[:, position]
        )

    # Gradient for worst-choice part:
    # because worst utilities are -beta, derivative is:
    # -chosen indicator plus softmax probabilities over exp(-beta).
    worst_u = -beta[remaining_idx]
    worst_prob = np.exp(worst_u - logsumexp(worst_u, axis=1, keepdims=True))

    np.add.at(grad_full, worst_idx, -1.0)

    for position in range(remaining_idx.shape[1]):
        np.add.at(
            grad_full,
            remaining_idx[:, position],
            worst_prob[:, position]
        )

    # Drop beta_1 because it is fixed to zero.
    return grad_full[1:]


def negative_log_likelihood(theta):
    return -mnl_log_likelihood(theta)


def negative_gradient(theta):
    return -mnl_gradient(theta)


# Estimate beta_2 through beta_10.
initial_theta = np.zeros(9)

mle_out = minimize(
    fun=negative_log_likelihood,
    x0=initial_theta,
    jac=negative_gradient,
    method="BFGS",
    options={
        "gtol": 1e-6,
        "maxiter": 10000
    }
)

assert mle_out.success, mle_out.message

theta_hat = mle_out.x
beta_hat = unpack_beta(theta_hat)
max_log_likelihood = mnl_log_likelihood(theta_hat)
```

```{python}
#| label: mle-standard-errors
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Numerical Hessian of the negative log-likelihood.
# Because we minimized the negative log-likelihood, its Hessian is the observed information matrix.

def finite_difference_hessian(func, x, eps=1e-4):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    k = len(x)
    hessian = np.zeros((k, k))
    f0 = func(x)

    for i in range(k):
        ei = np.zeros(k)
        ei[i] = eps

        f_plus = func(x + ei)
        f_minus = func(x - ei)

        hessian[i, i] = (f_plus - 2 * f0 + f_minus) / (eps ** 2)

        for j in range(i + 1, k):
            ej = np.zeros(k)
            ej[j] = eps

            f_pp = func(x + ei + ej)
            f_pm = func(x + ei - ej)
            f_mp = func(x - ei + ej)
            f_mm = func(x - ei - ej)

            hessian[i, j] = (f_pp - f_pm - f_mp + f_mm) / (4 * eps ** 2)
            hessian[j, i] = hessian[i, j]

    return hessian


hessian_neg_ll = finite_difference_hessian(
    negative_log_likelihood,
    theta_hat,
    eps=1e-4
)

try:
    cov_theta = np.linalg.inv(hessian_neg_ll)
except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
    cov_theta = np.linalg.pinv(hessian_neg_ll)

se_theta = np.sqrt(np.maximum(np.diag(cov_theta), 0))

# beta_1 is fixed to zero, so it does not have an estimated standard error.
se_full = np.concatenate(([np.nan], se_theta))

# Shares of preference
mle_share = np.exp(beta_hat - logsumexp(beta_hat))

mle_table = item_labels.copy()
mle_table["beta_hat"] = beta_hat
mle_table["se_beta"] = se_full
mle_table["mle_share"] = mle_share
mle_table["mle_rank"] = (
    mle_table["mle_share"]
    .rank(ascending=False, method="first")
    .astype(int)
)

mle_table = mle_table.sort_values("mle_rank").reset_index(drop=True)

mle_display = mle_table.copy()
mle_display["beta_hat"] = mle_display["beta_hat"].round(3)
mle_display["se_beta"] = mle_display["se_beta"].apply(
    lambda x: "Reference" if pd.isna(x) else f"{x:.3f}"
)
mle_display["mle_share"] = (100 * mle_display["mle_share"]).round(1).astype(str) + "%"

mle_display = mle_display.rename(columns={
    "item": "Item",
    "item_label": "Class",
    "beta_hat": "Beta hat",
    "se_beta": "SE",
    "mle_share": "Share of preference",
    "mle_rank": "MLE rank"
})

mle_display = mle_display[[
    "MLE rank",
    "Item",
    "Class",
    "Beta hat",
    "SE",
    "Share of preference"
]]

display(HTML(mle_display.to_html(index=False)))

display(Markdown(
    f"The MNL model converged successfully. "
    f"The maximized log-likelihood is **{max_log_likelihood:.2f}**."
))
```

## MNL via Bayesian Estimation

::: {.callout-}
I next estimate the same MNL model using Bayesian methods. The Bayesian model combines the likelihood from the previous section with a prior distribution over the utility coefficients. The posterior distribution is:

$$
\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \boldsymbol{y})
\propto
L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \cdot \pi(\boldsymbol{\beta})
$$

I use a weakly informative normal prior on the nine free coefficients:

$$
\beta_2, \ldots, \beta_{10} \sim N(0, 10)
$$

The prior standard deviation is $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.16$, which is fairly wide on the logit utility scale. As before, item 1 is the reference item, so $\beta_1 = 0$. I sample from the posterior using a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm.

```{python}
#| label: bayes-functions
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

from IPython.display import display, Markdown, HTML
from scipy.special import logsumexp
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as mtick

prior_sd = np.sqrt(10.0)

def log_prior(theta):
    theta = np.asarray(theta, dtype=float)

    return float(
        np.sum(
            -0.5 * np.log(2 * np.pi * prior_sd ** 2)
            - 0.5 * (theta / prior_sd) ** 2
        )
    )


def log_posterior(theta):
    return mnl_log_likelihood(theta) + log_prior(theta)


def metropolis_hastings(beta0, n_iter, step, seed=2025):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    beta0 = np.asarray(beta0, dtype=float)

    n_params = len(beta0)
    draws = np.empty((n_iter, n_params))

    beta_current = beta0.copy()
    log_post_current = log_posterior(beta_current)
    accept = 0

    for t in range(n_iter):
        beta_proposal = beta_current + rng.normal(0, step, size=n_params)
        log_post_proposal = log_posterior(beta_proposal)

        log_accept_ratio = log_post_proposal - log_post_current

        if np.log(rng.random()) < log_accept_ratio:
            beta_current = beta_proposal
            log_post_current = log_post_proposal
            accept += 1

        draws[t, :] = beta_current

    return {
        "draws": draws,
        "accept_rate": accept / n_iter
    }
```

I first tune the proposal step size with short pilot chains. The goal is an acceptance rate around 25% to 40%, which usually gives a reasonable balance between moving too slowly and rejecting too many proposals.

```{python}
#| label: bayes-tuning
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

pilot_steps = [0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12]
pilot_results = []

for i, step in enumerate(pilot_steps):
    pilot = metropolis_hastings(
        beta0=theta_hat,
        n_iter=2000,
        step=step,
        seed=1000 + i
    )

    pilot_results.append({
        "step_size": step,
        "acceptance_rate": pilot["accept_rate"]
    })

pilot_table = pd.DataFrame(pilot_results)
pilot_table["distance_from_target"] = (
    pilot_table["acceptance_rate"] - 0.30
).abs()

chosen_step = float(
    pilot_table
    .sort_values("distance_from_target")
    .iloc[0]["step_size"]
)

pilot_display = pilot_table.copy()
pilot_display["acceptance_rate"] = pilot_display["acceptance_rate"].round(3)
pilot_display["distance_from_target"] = pilot_display["distance_from_target"].round(3)

pilot_display = pilot_display.rename(columns={
    "step_size": "Step size",
    "acceptance_rate": "Pilot acceptance rate",
    "distance_from_target": "Distance from 30%"
})

display(HTML(pilot_display.to_html(index=False)))

display(Markdown(
    f"Based on the pilot chains, I use a final proposal step size of **{chosen_step:.2f}**."
))
```

Using the tuned step size, I run the final Metropolis-Hastings chain for 20,000 iterations and discard the first 25% as burn-in.

```{python}
#| label: run-bayes-mcmc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

n_iter = 20000
burn = int(0.25 * n_iter)

mcmc = metropolis_hastings(
    beta0=theta_hat,
    n_iter=n_iter,
    step=chosen_step,
    seed=403
)

draws = mcmc["draws"]
accept_rate = mcmc["accept_rate"]

mcmc_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": [
        "Iterations",
        "Burn-in draws",
        "Post-burn-in draws",
        "Proposal step size",
        "Final acceptance rate"
    ],
    "Value": [
        f"{n_iter:,}",
        f"{burn:,}",
        f"{n_iter - burn:,}",
        f"{chosen_step:.2f}",
        f"{accept_rate:.3f}"
    ]
})

display(HTML(mcmc_summary.to_html(index=False)))
```

The trace plots below show representative posterior draws for three utility coefficients. A good trace plot should look like a stable “fuzzy caterpillar,” meaning that the chain moves around a stable region rather than drifting upward or downward over time.

```{python}

#| echo: false

for ax, item in zip(axes, trace_items):
    theta_col = item - 2

    ax.set_title(short_name)

axes[-1].set_xlabel("MCMC iteration")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

After burn-in, I summarize the posterior draws. For each draw, I convert the utility coefficients into shares of preference using the softmax transformation. This allows me to report both posterior mean shares and 95% credible intervals for the shares.

```{python}
#| label: bayes-posterior-summary
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

post_draws = draws[burn:, :]

# Add beta_1 = 0 back into every posterior draw.
beta_draws = np.column_stack([
    np.zeros(post_draws.shape[0]),
    post_draws
])

# Convert every posterior draw into shares of preference.
share_draws = np.exp(
    beta_draws - logsumexp(beta_draws, axis=1, keepdims=True)
)

bayes_table = item_labels.sort_values("item").copy()

bayes_table["beta_mean_bayes"] = beta_draws.mean(axis=0)
bayes_table["beta_ci_lower"] = np.quantile(beta_draws, 0.025, axis=0)
bayes_table["beta_ci_upper"] = np.quantile(beta_draws, 0.975, axis=0)
bayes_table["beta_sd_bayes"] = beta_draws.std(axis=0, ddof=1)

bayes_table["share_mean_bayes"] = share_draws.mean(axis=0)
bayes_table["share_ci_lower"] = np.quantile(share_draws, 0.025, axis=0)
bayes_table["share_ci_upper"] = np.quantile(share_draws, 0.975, axis=0)

bayes_table["bayes_rank"] = (
    bayes_table["share_mean_bayes"]
    .rank(ascending=False, method="first")
    .astype(int)
)

bayes_table = bayes_table.sort_values("bayes_rank").reset_index(drop=True)

bayes_display = bayes_table.copy()

bayes_display["beta_mean_bayes"] = bayes_display["beta_mean_bayes"].round(3)
bayes_display["beta_ci"] = (
    "["
    + bayes_display["beta_ci_lower"].round(3).astype(str)
    + ", "
    + bayes_display["beta_ci_upper"].round(3).astype(str)
    + "]"
)

bayes_display["share_mean_bayes"] = (
    100 * bayes_display["share_mean_bayes"]
).round(1).astype(str) + "%"

bayes_display["share_ci"] = (
    "["
    + (100 * bayes_display["share_ci_lower"]).round(1).astype(str)
    + "%, "
    + (100 * bayes_display["share_ci_upper"]).round(1).astype(str)
    + "%]"
)

bayes_display = bayes_display.rename(columns={
    "bayes_rank": "Bayes rank",
    "item": "Item",
    "item_label": "Class",
    "beta_mean_bayes": "Posterior mean beta",
    "beta_ci": "95% beta credible interval",
    "share_mean_bayes": "Posterior mean share",
    "share_ci": "95% share credible interval"
})

bayes_display = bayes_display[[
    "Bayes rank",
    "Item",
    "Class",
    "Posterior mean beta",
    "95% beta credible interval",
    "Posterior mean share",
    "95% share credible interval"
]]

display(HTML(bayes_display.to_html(index=False)))
```

The Bayesian estimates are directly comparable to the maximum likelihood estimates. Because the prior is weak and the dataset is reasonably informative, the posterior means should be close to the MLE estimates. The main advantage of the Bayesian approach is that uncertainty for derived quantities, such as shares of preference, is easy to calculate by transforming every posterior draw.

```{python}
#| label: bayes-vs-mle-comparison
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

mle_for_bayes_compare = mle_table[[
    "item",
    "beta_hat",
    "se_beta",
    "mle_share",
    "mle_rank"
]].copy()

bayes_for_compare = bayes_table[[
    "item",
    "item_label",
    "beta_mean_bayes",
    "beta_sd_bayes",
    "share_mean_bayes",
    "bayes_rank"
]].copy()

mle_bayes_compare = (
    bayes_for_compare
    .merge(mle_for_bayes_compare, on="item", how="left")
)

mle_bayes_compare["abs_beta_difference"] = (
    mle_bayes_compare["beta_mean_bayes"]
    - mle_bayes_compare["beta_hat"]
).abs()

compare_display = mle_bayes_compare.copy()

compare_display["beta_hat"] = compare_display["beta_hat"].round(3)
compare_display["beta_mean_bayes"] = compare_display["beta_mean_bayes"].round(3)

compare_display["se_beta"] = compare_display["se_beta"].apply(
    lambda x: "Reference" if pd.isna(x) else f"{x:.3f}"
)

compare_display["beta_sd_bayes"] = compare_display["beta_sd_bayes"].apply(
    lambda x: "Fixed" if x == 0 else f"{x:.3f}"
)

compare_display["mle_share"] = (
    100 * compare_display["mle_share"]
).round(1).astype(str) + "%"

compare_display["share_mean_bayes"] = (
    100 * compare_display["share_mean_bayes"]
).round(1).astype(str) + "%"

compare_display = compare_display.sort_values("mle_rank")

compare_display = compare_display.rename(columns={
    "item": "Item",
    "item_label": "Class",
    "beta_hat": "MLE beta",
    "se_beta": "MLE SE",
    "beta_mean_bayes": "Bayes mean beta",
    "beta_sd_bayes": "Bayes posterior SD",
    "mle_share": "MLE share",
    "share_mean_bayes": "Bayes mean share",
    "mle_rank": "MLE rank",
    "bayes_rank": "Bayes rank"
})

compare_display = compare_display[[
    "Item",
    "Class",
    "MLE beta",
    "MLE SE",
    "Bayes mean beta",
    "Bayes posterior SD",
    "MLE share",
    "Bayes mean share",
    "MLE rank",
    "Bayes rank"
]]

display(HTML(compare_display.to_html(index=False)))

# Dynamic written comparison
free_compare = mle_bayes_compare[mle_bayes_compare["item"] != 1].copy()
largest_diff = free_compare.sort_values(
    "abs_beta_difference",
    ascending=False
).iloc[0]

top_bayes = bayes_table.iloc[0]
bottom_bayes = bayes_table.iloc[-1]

rank_changes = mle_bayes_compare[
    mle_bayes_compare["mle_rank"] != mle_bayes_compare["bayes_rank"]
].copy()

if len(rank_changes) == 0:
    rank_text = "The MLE and Bayesian rankings are identical."
else:
    changed_classes = ", ".join(rank_changes["item_label"].tolist())
    rank_text = (
        "The MLE and Bayesian rankings are very similar, with small rank changes for "
        f"{changed_classes}."
    )

display(Markdown(
    f"The Bayesian posterior ranking places **{top_bayes['item_label']}** first, "
    f"with a posterior mean share of **{100 * top_bayes['share_mean_bayes']:.1f}%**. "
    f"The lowest-ranked class is **{bottom_bayes['item_label']}**, "
    f"with a posterior mean share of **{100 * bottom_bayes['share_mean_bayes']:.1f}%**. "
    f"{rank_text} "
    f"The largest absolute difference between an MLE beta estimate and a Bayesian posterior mean beta is for "
    f"**{largest_diff['item_label']}**, but the difference is only **{largest_diff['abs_beta_difference']:.3f}**. "
    "Overall, the Bayesian results closely match the MLE results, while also giving credible intervals for the preference shares."
))
```
:::


## Comparing the Three Methods

::: {.callout-}
The three methods give three different views of the same MaxDiff preference data. The counts analysis is the simplest descriptive summary. The MLE MNL model estimates utilities and shares of preference using an explicit choice model. The Bayesian MNL model uses the same likelihood as the MLE model, but summarizes a full posterior distribution, which makes uncertainty easier to communicate.

```{python}
#| label: compare-three-methods-table
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

from IPython.display import display, Markdown, HTML
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as mtick

# Make sure ranks exist.
if "counts_rank" not in counts_table.columns:
    counts_table["counts_rank"] = (
        counts_table["score"]
        .rank(ascending=False, method="first")
        .astype(int)
    )

if "mle_rank" not in mle_table.columns:
    mle_table["mle_rank"] = (
        mle_table["mle_share"]
        .rank(ascending=False, method="first")
        .astype(int)
    )

if "bayes_rank" not in bayes_table.columns:
    bayes_table["bayes_rank"] = (
        bayes_table["share_mean_bayes"]
        .rank(ascending=False, method="first")
        .astype(int)
    )

# Combine counts, MLE, and Bayesian results into one comparison table.
compare_three = (
    counts_table[["item", "item_label", "score", "counts_rank"]]
    .merge(
        mle_table[["item", "mle_share", "mle_rank"]],
        on="item",
        how="left"
    )
    .merge(
        bayes_table[["item", "share_mean_bayes", "bayes_rank"]],
        on="item",
        how="left"
    )
)

compare_three = compare_three.sort_values("mle_rank").reset_index(drop=True)

compare_display = compare_three.copy()

compare_display["score"] = compare_display["score"].round(3)
compare_display["mle_share"] = (
    100 * compare_display["mle_share"]
).round(1).astype(str) + "%"
compare_display["share_mean_bayes"] = (
    100 * compare_display["share_mean_bayes"]
).round(1).astype(str) + "%"

compare_display = compare_display.rename(columns={
    "item": "Item",
    "item_label": "Class",
    "score": "Counts score",
    "counts_rank": "Counts rank",
    "mle_share": "MLE share",
    "mle_rank": "MLE rank",
    "share_mean_bayes": "Bayes mean share",
    "bayes_rank": "Bayes rank"
})

compare_display = compare_display[[
    "Item",
    "Class",
    "Counts score",
    "Counts rank",
    "MLE share",
    "MLE rank",
    "Bayes mean share",
    "Bayes rank"
]]

display(HTML(compare_display.to_html(index=False)))
```

The table is sorted by the MLE ranking. Overall, the three methods should tell a similar story, especially for the most preferred and least preferred classes. Differences are more likely to appear in the middle of the ranking, where several classes have similar preference strength.

```{python}
#| label: compare-three-methods-plot
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

plot_df = compare_three.copy()

plot_df["plot_label"] = plot_df["item_label"].str.replace(
    r"\s*\(.*?\)",
    "",
    regex=True
)

# Consistent color by item across all three panels.
items_sorted = sorted(plot_df["item"].unique())
cmap = plt.get_cmap("tab10")
item_colors = {
    item: cmap(i % 10)
    for i, item in enumerate(items_sorted)
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 7))

def draw_panel(ax, data, value_col, rank_col, title, xlabel, percent_axis=False, zero_line=False):
    # Sort so rank 1 appears at the top of the horizontal bar chart.
    d = data.sort_values(rank_col, ascending=False).copy()

    colors = [item_colors[item] for item in d["item"]]

    ax.barh(
        d["plot_label"],
        d[value_col],
        color=colors
    )

    if zero_line:
        ax.axvline(0, linewidth=1)

    if percent_axis:
        ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(1.0))

    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel("")
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=8)

draw_panel(
    axes[0],
    plot_df,
    value_col="score",
    rank_col="counts_rank",
    title="Counts Analysis",
    xlabel="Score: % best minus % worst",
    percent_axis=False,
    zero_line=True
)

draw_panel(
    axes[1],
    plot_df,
    value_col="mle_share",
    rank_col="mle_rank",
    title="MLE MNL",
    xlabel="Share of preference",
    percent_axis=True,
    zero_line=False
)

draw_panel(
    axes[2],
    plot_df,
    value_col="share_mean_bayes",
    rank_col="bayes_rank",
    title="Bayesian MNL",
    xlabel="Posterior mean share",
    percent_axis=True,
    zero_line=False
)

fig.suptitle("Comparison of Counts, MLE, and Bayesian MNL Results", fontsize=14)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: compare-three-methods-written-summary
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

def class_name(item):
    return compare_three.loc[
        compare_three["item"] == item,
        "item_label"
    ].iloc[0]

top_counts = compare_three.sort_values("counts_rank").iloc[0]["item"]
top_mle = compare_three.sort_values("mle_rank").iloc[0]["item"]
top_bayes = compare_three.sort_values("bayes_rank").iloc[0]["item"]

bottom_counts = compare_three.sort_values("counts_rank", ascending=False).iloc[0]["item"]
bottom_mle = compare_three.sort_values("mle_rank", ascending=False).iloc[0]["item"]
bottom_bayes = compare_three.sort_values("bayes_rank", ascending=False).iloc[0]["item"]

top_agree = (top_counts == top_mle == top_bayes)
bottom_agree = (bottom_counts == bottom_mle == bottom_bayes)

compare_three["max_rank_gap"] = compare_three[
    ["counts_rank", "mle_rank", "bayes_rank"]
].max(axis=1) - compare_three[
    ["counts_rank", "mle_rank", "bayes_rank"]
].min(axis=1)

largest_gaps = (
    compare_three
    .sort_values("max_rank_gap", ascending=False)
    .head(3)
)

largest_gap_text = ", ".join([
    f"{row['item_label']} with a maximum rank gap of {int(row['max_rank_gap'])}"
    for _, row in largest_gaps.iterrows()
])

if top_agree:
    top_sentence = (
        f"All three methods agree that the top-ranked class is "
        f"**{class_name(top_mle)}**."
    )
else:
    top_sentence = (
        "The three methods are very close at the top, but they do not select exactly the same first-ranked class. "
        f"Counts ranks **{class_name(top_counts)}** first, MLE ranks **{class_name(top_mle)}** first, "
        f"and Bayes ranks **{class_name(top_bayes)}** first."
    )

if bottom_agree:
    bottom_sentence = (
        f"All three methods also agree that the lowest-ranked class is "
        f"**{class_name(bottom_mle)}**."
    )
else:
    bottom_sentence = (
        "The bottom of the ranking is also similar, although not perfectly identical across methods. "
        f"Counts ranks **{class_name(bottom_counts)}** last, MLE ranks **{class_name(bottom_mle)}** last, "
        f"and Bayes ranks **{class_name(bottom_bayes)}** last."
    )

display(Markdown(
    f"{top_sentence} {bottom_sentence} "
    f"The largest ranking differences appear for {largest_gap_text}. "
    "These differences are mostly in the middle of the ranking, where several classes have similar estimated preference strength. "
    "The MNL model adds value over the counts analysis because it models the choice process explicitly: every item shown in a task contributes information, not only the items selected as best or worst. "
    "The Bayesian model adds a different kind of value by making uncertainty on derived quantities easy to summarize. "
    "For example, each posterior draw can be converted into a share of preference, and the distribution of those shares gives credible intervals directly."
))
```
:::


## Discussion

::: {.callout-}
Overall, the three methods tell a consistent story about MSBA class preferences. The strongest result is that **MGTA 495 Marketing Analytics** is the most preferred class in the survey. It has the highest simple counts score and also receives the largest share of preference in the MNL-based models. The next strongest classes are generally **MGTA 453 Business Analytics** and **MGTA 455 Customer Analytics**, suggesting that students are especially interested in courses that connect analytics directly to business and marketing decision-making.At the other end of the ranking, **MGTA 444 Analytics Consulting** is the least preferred class in the counts analysis and remains near the bottom in the MNL and Bayesian results. Other lower-ranked classes include **MGTA 451 Marketing/Finance/Operations** and **MGTA 403 AI Math, Programming, & Analytics**. This does not necessarily mean these classes are unimportant. Some may be more technical, more foundational, or less immediately attractive from a student-choice perspective. MaxDiff measures relative preference, not objective course value.Methodologically, the counts analysis is useful as a quick descriptive summary. It is easy to explain: for each class, we compare how often it was chosen as best versus how often it was chosen as worst. This makes counts analysis a good option for an executive dashboard or a first look at the data. However, it is less formal than the model-based approaches.The MLE MNL model is more rigorous because it models the actual choice process. Each task contributes information not only through the selected best and worst items, but also through the alternatives that were shown and not selected. The MNL results are helpful when we want formal utility estimates, standard errors, and shares of preference that can be compared across classes.The Bayesian MNL model gives very similar point estimates to the MLE model, which is reassuring. Its main advantage is uncertainty quantification. Because the Bayesian approach produces posterior draws, it is straightforward to transform every draw into shares of preference and then summarize uncertainty with credible intervals. This would be especially useful for simulations, such as predicting demand for a new class or estimating how preferences might change if the course menu changed.There are several caveats. The survey respondents are a self-selected sample of MSBA students, so the results may not generalize to all students or future cohorts. Preferences may also depend on prior coursework, career goals, current academic standing, instructor reputation, and how familiar students are with each course. In addition, the order and wording of class descriptions may affect how students interpret the choices.If I had more time, I would extend the model to estimate individual-level preferences rather than only aggregate preferences. A hierarchical Bayesian model would be useful because it could show whether different groups of students prefer different types of classes. I would also collect background information such as career interest, technical experience, and program stage to better explain why students prefer certain classes over others.
:::
